subtitles.text: Jesus continued. There was a man who had two sons.
The younger one said to his father, Father, give me my share of the estate.
So he divided his property between them.
Not long after that, the younger son got together all he had, set off for a distant country
and there squandered his wealth in wild living.
After he had spent everything, there was a severe famine in that whole country, and he began to be in need.
So he went and hired himself out to a citizen of that country, who sent him to his fields to feed pigs.
He longed to fill his stomach with the pods that the pigs were eating, but no one gave him anything.
When he came to his senses, he said, How many of my father's hired servants have food to spare,
and here I am starving to death!
I will set out and go back to my father and say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you.
I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired servants.
So he got up and went to his father.
But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion for him;
he ran to his son, threw his arms around him and kissed him.
The son said to him, Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you.
I am no longer worthy to be called your son.
But the father said to his servants, Quick! Bring the best robe and put it on him.
Put a ring on his finger and sandals on his feet.
Bring the fattened calf and kill it. Let's have a feast and celebrate.
For this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.
So they began to celebrate.
Meanwhile, the older son was in the field.
When he came near the house, he heard music and dancing.
So he called one of the servants and asked him what was going on.
Your brother has come, he replied, and your father has killed the fattened calf
because he has him back safe and sound.
The older brother became angry and refused to go in.
So his father went out and pleaded with him.
But he answered his father, Look! All these years I've been slaving for you and never disobeyed your orders.
Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends.
But when this son of yours who has squandered your property with prostitutes comes home,
you kill the fattened calf for him!
My son, the father said, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours.
But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours
was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.

introParts: A faithful son stands outside his father's party.
His brother squandered it all and wears the best robe.
In this devotional, one word in the father's reply about the feast.
The father steps out to him.
cards.hookText:
A faithful son stands outside his father's party.

His brother squandered it all and wears the best robe.

In this devotional, one word in the father's reply about the feast.

The father steps out to him.

Let's watch.

cards.text: Picture the older son coming in from the field.
His back aches.
His hands are dirty.
And the house is full of music and dancing.
Nobody came to tell him.
He has to ask a servant what is going on.
cards.highlight: He has to ask a servant what is going on.

cards.text: He stops at the door.
Many of us who have served a long time know exactly where he is standing.
His case is real.
He stayed.
He obeyed.
His brother took his share of everything the family owned and burned through it far from home.
Now the one who wasted it all gets the party.
Look at where the younger son had ended up.
Feeding pigs.
For a Jewish listener, swine were regarded as the most unclean and the most abhorred of all animals.
This boy had fallen about as far from his father's house as a son could fall.
So the older brother is not angry over nothing.
That is the son being welcomed.
The one who longed to eat what the pigs were eating.
Now look at how he was welcomed.
The best robe is brought out.
cards.highlight: The best robe is brought out.

cards.text: In a household, producing the best robe was a mark of special honor.
Then the fattened calf.
Animals were rarely slaughtered except for a guest or a feast.
The father did not quietly slip his son back in as a hired hand.
He honored him in front of the whole household.
cards.highlight: He honored him in front of the whole household.

cards.text: And that is the very thing the older son cannot bear.
Jesus tells this story to Pharisees and scribes who were grumbling because he ate with sinners.
The older brother is their portrait.
But he is also a portrait of people in the church in every age, who worry that the door of grace is open too wide.
That spirit grows from forgetting how much we ourselves have been given.
Someone who knows he stands only by grace does not talk like the older brother.
Now notice the father.
Earlier he ran to the son who came home.
Here he walks out to the son who never left.
He does not scold.
He pleads.
Son, you are always with me.
All that is mine is yours.
In verse 32 the father says it was fitting to celebrate.

Then the story simply stops.

Jesus leaves the door open, and the Pharisees standing in it.

The Father who runs to the wanderer also comes out to plead with the worker.

cards.verse: For this son of mine was dead and is alive again! He was lost and is found!’ So they began to celebrate.

questions: Whose homecoming to God would you find hardest to celebrate, and where are you standing while the music plays?
cards.prayer: Tell God about the person whose forgiveness you have quietly resented. Ask him for his own gladness over them.

paragraphs.text: Picture the older son coming in from the field. His back aches. His hands are dirty. And the house is full of music and dancing. Nobody came to tell him. He has to ask a servant what is going on. He stops at the door. Many of us who have served a long time know exactly where he is standing.
His case is real. He stayed. He obeyed. His brother took his share of everything the family owned and burned through it far from home. Now the one who wasted it all gets the party.

Look at where the younger son had ended up. Feeding pigs. For a Jewish listener, swine were regarded as the most unclean and the most abhorred of all animals. This boy had fallen about as far from his father's house as a son could fall.
So the older brother is not angry over nothing. That is the son being welcomed. The one who longed to eat what the pigs were eating.

Now look at how he was welcomed. The best robe is brought out. In a household, producing the best robe was a mark of special honor. Then the fattened calf. Animals were rarely slaughtered except for a guest or a feast.
The father did not quietly slip his son back in as a hired hand. He honored him in front of the whole household. And that is the very thing the older son cannot bear.

Jesus tells this story to Pharisees and scribes who were grumbling because he ate with sinners. The older brother is their portrait. But he is also a portrait of people in the church in every age, who worry that the door of grace is open too wide. That spirit grows from forgetting how much we ourselves have been given. Someone who knows he stands only by grace does not talk like the older brother.
Now notice the father. Earlier he ran to the son who came home. Here he walks out to the son who never left. He does not scold. He pleads. Son, you are always with me. All that is mine is yours.
In verse 32 the father says it was fitting to celebrate. The word Luke uses there carries necessity. It means one must. This had to happen.
The father is not saying the feast was a nice touch. He is saying that when a dead son comes alive, celebration is not optional.
The return of any soul ought to bring joy to everyone who sees it. The only questions worth asking are these. Is he home? Was the dead one made alive? If so, gladness is the right answer.
Then the story simply stops. We never hear whether the older son went in. Jesus leaves the door open, and the Pharisees standing in it. He leaves us standing there too.

Inside, Christ is at the table with sinners. The music is already playing. And the Father's plea to his faithful children is the same gift he gave the wanderer: his own gladness, waiting for them to share it.
